records.source: וַיְהִ֣י אַֽחֲרֵי־כֵ֗ן וּלְאַבְשָׁל֧וֹם בֶּן־דָּוִ֛ד אָח֥וֹת יָפָ֖ה וּשְׁמָ֣הּ תָּמָ֑ר וַיֶּאֱהָבֶ֖הָ אַמְנ֥וֹן בֶּן־דָּוִֽד׃
records.gloss: And it was after this, and to Absalom son of David [was] a sister beautiful, and her name [was] Tamar; and loved her Amnon son of David.
pieces: Some time after this, Absalom son of David had a beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon son of David fell in love with her.

L.1: And it happened after this: Absalom the son of David had a beautiful sister, and her name [was] Tamar, and Amnon the son of David loved her.

R.1: Later on, David's son Absalom had a beautiful sister named Tamar. Another of David's sons, Amnon, fell in love with her.

decisions.choice: Absalom and Tamar: full brother and sister; Amnon: their half-brother
decisions.reason: Absalom was David's son by Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (3:3), and Tamar was his full sister. Amnon was David's firstborn, the son of Ahinoam (3:2), so he was Tamar's half-brother and the heir to the throne. Calling both young men "son of David" sets them side by side as rivals within one house.

decisions.choice: loved her: desired her
decisions.reason: The verb covers every kind of love and attraction. What follows shows that Amnon's "love" was desire for her, which turns into hatred once he has had his way (verse 15).

decisions.choice: after this: the trouble foretold to David begins
decisions.reason: The phrase loosely links this story to what came before. Nathan had told David that the sword would never leave his house and that trouble would rise against him from within it (12:10-11). Chapters 13-18 tell how that came about through David's own sons.

decisions.choice: Another of David's sons
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that Amnon is a second son of David, not Tamar's full brother; the Hebrew does this by repeating "son of David".

records.heading: Amnon and Tamar

records.source: וַיֵּ֨צֶר לְאַמְנ֜וֹן לְהִתְחַלּ֗וֹת בַּֽעֲבוּר֙ תָּמָ֣ר אֲחֹת֔וֹ כִּ֥י בְתוּלָ֖ה הִ֑יא וַיִּפָּלֵא֙ בְּעֵינֵ֣י אַמְנ֔וֹן לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת לָ֖הּ מְאֽוּמָה׃
records.gloss: And it was distress to Amnon to the point of making himself sick because of Tamar his sister, for a virgin [was] she, and it was too difficult in [the] eyes of Amnon to do to her anything.
pieces: Amnon was so tormented over his sister Tamar that he made himself ill. She was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.

L.2: And Amnon was so distressed that he made himself sick because of Tamar his sister, for she [was] a virgin, and it was too difficult in the eyes of Amnon to do anything to her.

R.2: Amnon wanted Tamar so badly that he made himself sick over her. She was a virgin, and Amnon thought there was no way he could do anything with her.

decisions.choice: made himself sick: he became ill from his obsession
decisions.reason: The verb form can mean to make oneself sick or to pretend to be sick, as it does in verses 5 and 6. Here it describes how Amnon's frustrated desire wore him down until he was ill; verse 4 shows that it could be seen in his face. Some take it to mean he was already acting sick, but the pretending is Jonadab's idea in verse 5.

decisions.choice: she was a virgin: an unmarried daughter of the king, closely guarded
decisions.reason: A king's unmarried daughters lived in their own quarters and wore a robe that marked them out (verse 18). Amnon could not see her alone without arousing suspicion. The words also show what he wanted: not to marry her but to have her.

decisions.choice: too difficult in his eyes: it seemed impossible to him
decisions.reason: The verb is used of what is beyond someone's power (Genesis 18:14; Deuteronomy 30:11). "In his eyes" means in his own judgment.

decisions.choice: tormented (Balanced); wanted Tamar so badly (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says it was "distress" or "tightness" for Amnon. Balanced says "tormented"; Readable says plainly what the distress was about.

records.source: וּלְאַמְנ֣וֹן רֵ֗עַ וּשְׁמוֹ֙ יֽוֹנָדָ֔ב בֶּן־שִׁמְעָ֖ה אֲחִ֣י דָוִ֑ד וְי֣וֹנָדָ֔ב אִ֥ישׁ חָכָ֖ם מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: And to Amnon [was] a friend, and his name [was] Jonadab son of Shimeah, brother of David; and Jonadab [was] a man shrewd very.
pieces: Now Amnon had a friend named Jonadab son of Shimeah, David's brother. Jonadab was a very shrewd man.

L.3: And Amnon had a friend, and his name [was] Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab [was] a very shrewd man.

R.3: Amnon had a friend named Jonadab. He was the son of Shimeah, David's brother, so he was Amnon's cousin. Jonadab was a very clever and crafty man.

decisions.choice: shrewd: clever in practical matters, here in a crafty way
decisions.reason: The word usually translated "wise" covers skill of every kind, good or bad. Jonadab's wisdom is cleverness in getting things done; he uses it to plan a crime. The same word describes the woman Joab sends to trick David (14:2).

decisions.choice: Shimeah, David's brother: Jonadab was Amnon's cousin
decisions.reason: Shimeah is the brother called Shammah and Shimea elsewhere, the third son of Jesse (1 Samuel 16:9; 17:13; 1 Chronicles 2:13). His son Jonathan killed a giant at Gath (21:21).

decisions.choice: a friend: a close companion
decisions.reason: The word means a friend or companion. At David's court "the king's friend" was also a title for a trusted adviser (15:37; 16:16), and it may hint that Jonadab was Amnon's confidant at court.

decisions.choice: so he was Amnon's cousin; clever and crafty
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the family tie and uses two words for the one Hebrew word, so that young readers do not take "wise" as praise here.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ מַדּ֣וּעַ אַ֠תָּה כָּ֣כָה דַּ֤ל בֶּן־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ בַּבֹּ֣קֶר בַּבֹּ֔קֶר הֲל֖וֹא תַּגִּ֣יד לִ֑י וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ אַמְנ֔וֹן אֶת־תָּמָ֗ר אֲח֛וֹת אַבְשָׁלֹ֥ם אָחִ֖י אֲנִ֥י אֹהֵֽב׃
records.gloss: And he said to him, why [are] you thus weak, son of the king, in the morning, in the morning? Will you not tell me? And said to him Amnon, Tamar [the] sister of Absalom my brother I [am] loving.
pieces: He asked him, "Why do you look so worn out, son of the king, morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon answered him, "I am in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."

L.4: And he said to him, "Why [are] you so haggard, son of the king, morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" And Amnon said to him, "Tamar, the sister of Absalom my brother, I love."

R.4: Jonadab asked him, "You are the king's son! Why do you look so thin and miserable every morning? Tell me what is wrong." Amnon answered, "I am in love with Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom."

decisions.choice: haggard: thin and worn down
decisions.reason: The word means poor, thin or weak. It is used of Pharaoh's thin cows (Genesis 41:19). Amnon's longing shows in his body.

decisions.choice: in the morning, in the morning: day after day
decisions.reason: Repeating a word in this way means "every" (Exodus 16:21). Jonadab sees him every morning looking worse.

decisions.choice: Tamar, the sister of Absalom my brother: Amnon names her by Absalom
decisions.reason: Amnon puts Tamar first, and calls her Absalom's sister rather than his own. He keeps her at a distance from himself as he speaks, and Absalom's name already stands in the story as the brother who will act for her.

decisions.choice: I am in love with Tamar
decisions.reason: Literal keeps Tamar's name first, as the Hebrew does. Balanced and Readable use ordinary English order. Readable turns the opening question into an exclamation and the second question into a request.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ יְה֣וֹנָדָ֔ב שְׁכַ֥ב עַל־מִשְׁכָּבְךָ֖ וְהִתְחָ֑ל וּבָ֧א אָבִ֣יךָ לִרְאוֹתֶ֗ךָ וְאָמַרְתָּ֣ אֵלָ֡יו תָּ֣בֹא נָא֩ תָמָ֨ר אֲחוֹתִ֜י וְתַבְרֵ֣נִי לֶ֗חֶם וְעָשְׂתָ֤ה לְעֵינַי֙ אֶת־הַבִּרְיָ֔ה לְמַ֨עַן֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֶרְאֶ֔ה וְאָכַלְתִּ֖י מִיָּדָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And said to him Jonadab, lie on your bed and make yourself sick, and [when] comes your father to see you, and you will say to him, let come please Tamar my sister and let her give me to eat food, and let her make before my eyes the food, so that I may see, and I will eat from her hand.
pieces: Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. Then, when your father comes to visit you, tell him, 'I beg you, let my sister Tamar come and feed me. Have her prepare the food here in front of me, so that I can watch and then eat it from her hand.'"

L.5: And Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. And when your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Please let Tamar my sister come and give me food to eat, and let her prepare the food in my sight, so that I may see [it] and eat from her hand.'"

R.5: Jonadab told him, "Go to bed and act as if you are sick. Your father will come to see how you are. Ask him, 'Would you let my sister Tamar come and bring me something to eat? I want her to make the food here where I can watch her. Then I will eat it from her hand.'"

decisions.choice: make yourself sick: pretend to be ill
decisions.reason: The same verb form as in verse 2, here plainly meaning to act the part of a sick man, as verse 6 confirms.

decisions.choice: give me food to eat; the food: a meal brought to someone sick or grieving
decisions.reason: The verb and the noun come from a root used of food given to the sick or the mourning (3:35; 12:17). A sick man asking for a meal from his sister's hand would not seem strange to the king.

decisions.choice: Jonadab: the Hebrew here spells the name in a longer form
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has Jehonadab, the full form of the name, with the divine name as its first part. It is the same man as in verse 3.

decisions.choice: Jonadab
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the spelling of verse 3, so that readers do not think a second man has come in.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁכַּ֥ב אַמְנ֖וֹן וַיִּתְחָ֑ל וַיָּבֹ֨א הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לִרְאֹת֗וֹ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אַמְנ֤וֹן אֶל־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ תָּֽבוֹא־נָ֞א תָּמָ֣ר אֲחֹתִ֗י וּתְלַבֵּ֤ב לְעֵינַי֙ שְׁתֵּ֣י לְבִב֔וֹת וְאֶבְרֶ֖ה מִיָּדָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And lay down Amnon and made himself sick, and came the king to see him, and said Amnon to the king, let come please Tamar my sister and let her make cakes before my eyes, two cakes, and I will eat from her hand.
pieces: So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to him, "I beg you, let my sister Tamar come here and make a couple of cakes in front of me, so that I can eat from her hand."

L.6: So Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. And the king came to see him, and Amnon said to the king, "Please let Tamar my sister come and make two cakes in my sight, and I will eat from her hand."

R.6: So Amnon went to bed and pretended to be sick. The king came to visit him, and Amnon said, "Please send my sister Tamar to me. Let her make two cakes while I watch. Then I can eat them from her hand."

decisions.choice: make cakes; cakes: a kind of cake, perhaps heart-shaped
decisions.reason: The verb and the noun are built from the word for "heart", and are found only in this story. They may name heart-shaped cakes, or cakes thought to give strength. Elsewhere the same verb means "you have captured my heart" (Song of Songs 4:9), so the words may also hint at Amnon's desire.

decisions.choice: two cakes: a small amount
decisions.reason: Asking for just two cakes makes the request sound modest and harmless.

decisions.choice: a couple of cakes
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the sense of the small number; Literal and Readable keep "two".

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֥ח דָּוִ֛ד אֶל־תָּמָ֖ר הַבַּ֣יְתָה לֵאמֹ֑ר לְכִ֣י נָ֗א בֵּ֚ית אַמְנ֣וֹן אָחִ֔יךְ וַעֲשִׂי־ל֖וֹ הַבִּרְיָֽה׃
records.gloss: And sent David to Tamar to the house, saying, go please [to the] house of Amnon your brother and make for him the food.
pieces: David sent word to Tamar at the palace: "Please go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare some food for him."

L.7: And David sent to Tamar at the house, saying, "Please go to the house of Amnon your brother and prepare the food for him."

R.7: So David sent a message to Tamar at the palace. It said, "Please go to your brother Amnon's house and make some food for him."

decisions.choice: the house: the royal palace
decisions.reason: "The house" here is the king's house, where Tamar lived. The king's grown sons had houses of their own (verse 8; 14:24).

decisions.choice: David sent: the king himself sends her
decisions.reason: The plan works through David's own order. He does not suspect anything, and Tamar goes because her father has told her to.

decisions.choice: the palace
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "palace" for "the house", since it was the king's.

records.source: וַתֵּ֣לֶךְ תָּמָ֗ר בֵּ֛ית אַמְנ֥וֹן אָחִ֖יהָ וְה֣וּא שֹׁכֵ֑ב וַתִּקַּ֨ח אֶת־הַבָּצֵ֤ק וַתָּ֨לָשׁ֙ וַתְּלַבֵּ֣ב לְעֵינָ֔יו וַתְּבַשֵּׁ֖ל אֶת־הַלְּבִבֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And went Tamar [to the] house of Amnon her brother, and he [was] lying down; and she took the dough and kneaded and made cakes before his eyes, and baked the cakes.
pieces: So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying in bed. She took dough, kneaded it, made cakes while he watched, and baked them.

L.8: And Tamar went to the house of Amnon her brother, and he [was] lying down. And she took the dough and kneaded [it] and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes.

R.8: So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house. He was lying in bed. She took some dough and kneaded it. She shaped it into cakes while he watched, and she cooked them.

decisions.choice: baked: cooked
decisions.reason: The verb means to cook in general, by boiling or baking. With cakes of dough, baking or frying is meant.

decisions.choice: kneaded: the written and the read forms differ only in spelling
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text writes this verb one way in its letters and its scribes' notes read it another way. Both forms mean "she kneaded"; nothing in the sense changes.

decisions.choice: she took, kneaded, made, baked: each step told
decisions.reason: The run of short verbs slows the story and shows Tamar doing all that she was asked, in full view of Amnon.

records.source: וַתִּקַּ֤ח אֶת־הַמַּשְׂרֵת֙ וַתִּצֹ֣ק לְפָנָ֔יו וַיְמָאֵ֖ן לֶאֱכ֑וֹל וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אַמְנ֗וֹן הוֹצִ֤יאוּ כָל־אִישׁ֙ מֵֽעָלַ֔י וַיֵּצְא֥וּ כָל־אִ֖ישׁ מֵעָלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And she took the pan and poured out before him, and he refused to eat; and said Amnon, send out every man from with me; and went out every man from with him.
pieces: Then she took the pan and set the cakes out before him, but he refused to eat. "Send everyone out of here," Amnon said, and they all left him.

L.9: And she took the pan and poured [them] out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send everyone out from me." And everyone went out from him.

R.9: Then she took the pan and served him the cakes, but he would not eat. Amnon said, "Make everyone leave!" So everyone went out.

decisions.choice: the pan; poured out: she tipped the cakes out of the pan
decisions.reason: The word for the pan is found only here, so its exact shape is not known. "Poured out" suggests she turned the cakes out of it in front of him.

decisions.choice: send everyone out from me: the words Joseph used
decisions.reason: Joseph gave the same order before he made himself known to his brothers (Genesis 45:1). There it cleared the room for a family reunion; here it clears the room for a crime against a sister.

decisions.choice: every man: everyone present
decisions.reason: The phrase means every person there, chiefly the servants. Tamar is left alone with Amnon.

decisions.choice: set the cakes out (Balanced); served him the cakes (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not name what she poured out; Balanced and Readable name the cakes.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אַמְנ֜וֹן אֶל־תָּמָ֗ר הָבִ֤יאִי הַבִּרְיָה֙ הַחֶ֔דֶר וְאֶבְרֶ֖ה מִיָּדֵ֑ךְ וַתִּקַּ֣ח תָּמָ֗ר אֶת־הַלְּבִבוֹת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֔תָה וַתָּבֵ֛א לְאַמְנ֥וֹן אָחִ֖יהָ הֶחָֽדְרָה׃
records.gloss: And said Amnon to Tamar, bring the food [into] the chamber, and I will eat from your hand. And took Tamar the cakes which she had made and brought [them] to Amnon her brother to the chamber.
pieces: Amnon then told Tamar, "Bring the food in here to the bedroom, and I will eat from your hand." So Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom.

L.10: And Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the inner room, so that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar took the cakes that she had made and brought [them] to Amnon her brother into the inner room.

R.10: Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into my bedroom. I want you to feed me." So Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in his bedroom.

decisions.choice: the chamber: an inner, private room, here his bedroom
decisions.reason: The word names a room further inside a house, out of sight (Genesis 43:30). With Amnon lying sick, it is the room where he slept (Exodus 7:28 speaks of a "bedroom" with the same word).

decisions.choice: Amnon her brother: the narrator keeps calling him her brother
decisions.reason: "Her brother" is repeated through the story (verses 4, 7, 8, 10, 12). The repetition makes plain the bond Amnon is about to violate.

decisions.choice: the bedroom
decisions.reason: Literal says "inner room", the general sense; Balanced and Readable say "bedroom", the room meant here. Readable puts "eat from your hand" as "feed me".

records.source: וַתַּגֵּ֥שׁ אֵלָ֖יו לֶֽאֱכֹ֑ל וַיַּֽחֲזֶק־בָּהּ֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָ֔הּ בּ֛וֹאִי שִׁכְבִ֥י עִמִּ֖י אֲחוֹתִֽי׃
records.gloss: And she brought [them] near to him to eat, and he seized her and said to her, come, lie with me, my sister.
pieces: But when she brought them close for him to eat, he grabbed her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."

L.11: And she brought [them] near to him to eat, and he seized her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."

R.11: But when she held the food out to him, he grabbed her. He said, "Come to bed with me, my sister."

decisions.choice: seized her: took hold of her by force
decisions.reason: The verb means to grasp firmly. It is the verb of the law on a man who seizes a woman in the countryside (Deuteronomy 22:25).

decisions.choice: come, lie with me: the words of Potiphar's wife
decisions.reason: Potiphar's wife said the same words when she seized Joseph (Genesis 39:7, 12). Joseph got away; Tamar cannot.

decisions.choice: my sister: the relationship the law forbade
decisions.reason: The law forbade sexual relations with a sister or half-sister (Leviticus 18:9, 11; 20:17; Deuteronomy 27:22). Amnon calls her "my sister" in the very words that ask for what the law forbids.

decisions.choice: Come to bed with me
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what Amnon is asking, in words that a young reader can follow without being graphic.

records.source: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ אַל־אָחִי֙ אַל־תְּעַנֵּ֔נִי כִּ֛י לֹא־יֵֽעָשֶׂ֥ה כֵ֖ן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל אַֽל־תַּעֲשֵׂ֖ה אֶת־הַנְּבָלָ֥ה הַזֹּֽאת׃
records.gloss: And she said to him, no, my brother, do not humble me, for not it is done thus in Israel; do not do the disgraceful thing, this.
pieces: "No, my brother!" she said to him. "Do not violate me! Such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this outrageous thing.

L.12: And she said to him, "No, my brother! Do not humble me, for such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing.

R.12: "No, my brother!" she said. "Do not force me! A thing like this must never be done in Israel. Do not do this shameful thing.

decisions.choice: humble me: violate me, take my honor by force
decisions.reason: The verb means to humble, degrade or violate. It is used of the rape of Dinah (Genesis 34:2) and in the law on a man who seizes a woman (Deuteronomy 22:29). Here it names the wrong Amnon is about to do to her; it returns in verses 14, 22 and 32.

decisions.choice: disgraceful thing: an outrage that shames the whole people
decisions.reason: The word is used of a gross wrong, often a sexual one, that breaks the bonds of the community: the rape of Dinah (Genesis 34:7), the outrage at Gibeah (Judges 19:23; 20:6) and the case in Deuteronomy 22:21.

decisions.choice: it is not done thus in Israel: Tamar appeals to the people's own standard
decisions.reason: Her words echo what Jacob's sons said after Dinah was raped: "such a thing is not done" (Genesis 34:7). Tamar reminds Amnon that this is not just a private act but a crime against Israel's way of life.

decisions.choice: humble (Literal); violate (Balanced); force (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "humble" and Balanced says "violate", as in Deuteronomy 22:29, where a man also takes hold of the woman. Readable says "force" here, and "rape" when the act is told (verses 14, 22, 32), since the story makes plain that force was used (as Judges 20:5 says "raped"); Deuteronomy 22 says "dishonored" at Readable, where the law covers more than one case.

decisions.choice: outrageous thing (Balanced); shameful thing (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in Deuteronomy 22:21, Balanced says "outrageous" and Readable says "shameful". Literal keeps "disgraceful", as in Genesis 34:7.

records.source: וַאֲנִ֗י אָ֤נָה אוֹלִיךְ֙ אֶת־חֶרְפָּתִ֔י וְאַתָּ֗ה תִּהְיֶ֛ה כְּאַחַ֥ד הַנְּבָלִ֖ים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְעַתָּה֙ דַּבֶּר־נָ֣א אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּ֛י לֹ֥א יִמְנָעֵ֖נִי מִמֶּֽךָּ׃
records.gloss: And I, where will I carry my disgrace? And you, you will be like one of the fools in Israel. And now speak please to the king, for not will he withhold me from you.
pieces: As for me, where could I go with my shame? And you would be counted among the outrageous fools in Israel. Now please, speak to the king. He will not keep me from you."

L.13: And I, where would I carry my disgrace? And you, you would be like one of the disgraceful fools in Israel. And now, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you."

R.13: Where could I go? I would have to live with this disgrace. And people would think of you as one of the worst fools in Israel. Please, just talk to the king. He will let you marry me."

decisions.choice: where would I carry my disgrace: there would be nowhere I could go with my shame
decisions.reason: The question expects no answer. A woman raped and then left unmarried bore a shame that would follow her for life; verse 20 shows that this is what happened.

decisions.choice: the fools: people who are morally reckless and shameless
decisions.reason: The word is related to "disgraceful thing" in verse 12. It does not mean dull or slow, but someone who acts without regard for God or for others, like Nabal, whose name means "fool" (1 Samuel 25:25). Amnon, the heir to the throne, would be counted among the worst of men.

decisions.choice: he will not withhold me from you: the king would let you marry me
decisions.reason: The law forbade marriage with a half-sister (Leviticus 18:9, 11; 20:17), though in the time of the ancestors Abraham had married his (Genesis 20:12). The text does not say whether Tamar thought David would really allow it or was saying anything she could to escape. Either way, she offers Amnon a lawful way and he refuses it.

decisions.choice: I would have to live with this disgrace; He will let you marry me
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the question into a question and a statement of what it implies, and says plainly that "he will not withhold me from you" means marriage.

records.source: וְלֹ֥א אָבָ֖ה לִשְׁמֹ֣עַ בְּקוֹלָ֑הּ וַיֶּחֱזַ֤ק מִמֶּ֨נָּה֙ וַיְעַנֶּ֔הָ וַיִּשְׁכַּ֖ב אֹתָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: But not he was willing to listen to her voice, and he was stronger than her, and he humbled her and lay her.
pieces: But he would not listen to her. He was stronger than she was, and he violated her and lay with her by force.

L.14: But he was not willing to listen to her voice; and he was stronger than she, and he humbled her and lay with her.

R.14: But Amnon would not listen to her. He was stronger than she was, and he raped her.

decisions.choice: he was stronger than she: he overpowered her
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in verse 11, "he seized her", here with "than her": he used his strength against her. The text leaves no doubt that she did not consent.

decisions.choice: humbled her and lay her: he raped her
decisions.reason: The verb "humble" is the one of verse 12. "Lay her" is written with the mark of a direct object instead of the usual "lay with her", as in the rape of Dinah (Genesis 34:2); the wording presents her as acted upon, not as a partner. Together the verbs describe rape, as in Deuteronomy 22:25.

decisions.choice: he was not willing to listen to her voice: her plea is refused
decisions.reason: Tamar had spoken at length (verses 12-13); Amnon does not answer her. The same words return in verse 16, when he refuses to listen a second time.

decisions.choice: violated her and lay with her by force (Balanced); raped her (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew verbs. Balanced keeps "violated" for the verb of verse 12 and adds "by force" for the wording of "lay her" and the overpowering just described. Readable says in one plain word what the verbs together describe. The text tells the act soberly, and the English does the same.

records.source: וַיִּשְׂנָאֶ֣הָ אַמְנ֗וֹן שִׂנְאָה֙ גְּדוֹלָ֣ה מְאֹ֔ד כִּ֣י גְדוֹלָ֗ה הַשִּׂנְאָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שְׂנֵאָ֔הּ מֵאַהֲבָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֲהֵבָ֑הּ וַֽיֹּאמֶר־לָ֥הּ אַמְנ֖וֹן ק֥וּמִי לֵֽכִי׃
records.gloss: And hated her Amnon [with] hatred great very, for greater [was] the hatred which he hated her than the love which he had loved her. And said to her Amnon, get up, go.
pieces: Then Amnon turned on her with a fierce hatred. What he felt against her now was stronger than the love he had once felt for her. "Get up and go!" Amnon said to her.

L.15: And Amnon hated her [with] a very great hatred, for the hatred with which he hated her [was] greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up, go!"

R.15: Then Amnon began to hate Tamar bitterly. His hatred for her was even stronger than his love had been. He said to her, "Get up and get out!"

decisions.choice: hated her with a very great hatred: the hatred is stressed
decisions.reason: The words "hate" and "hatred" come four times in the verse, "love" twice. The repetition shows how completely Amnon's desire has turned to loathing.

decisions.choice: the love with which he had loved her: his desire for her
decisions.reason: The love of verse 1 is shown to have been desire, which ended once he had used her.

decisions.choice: get up, go: a curt dismissal
decisions.reason: Two bare commands, without her name or any courtesy. He speaks to her as one would drive off someone unwanted.

decisions.choice: What he felt against her now was stronger than the love he had once felt
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable shorten the repeated "hatred with which he hated her" so the comparison reads clearly; Literal keeps the repetition. Readable says "get out" for the second command, its sense here.

records.source: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ אַל־אוֹדֹ֞ת הָרָעָ֤ה הַגְּדוֹלָה֙ הַזֹּ֔את מֵאַחֶ֛רֶת אֲשֶׁר־עָשִׂ֥יתָ עִמִּ֖י לְשַׁלְּחֵ֑נִי וְלֹ֥א אָבָ֖ה לִשְׁמֹ֥עַֽ לָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And she said to him, no, because of this great evil, more than [the] other which you did with me, to send me away. But not he was willing to listen to her.
pieces: "No!" she said to him. "Sending me away would be a greater wrong than what you have already done to me." But he would not listen to her.

L.16: And she said to him, "No! For this great wrong, sending me away, [is worse] than the other that you have done to me." But he was not willing to listen to her.

R.16: "No!" she said. "Sending me away is even worse than what you have already done to me." But he would not listen to her.

decisions.choice: the Hebrew text, read as: "No, for this great wrong of sending me away is worse than the other you did to me"
alternatives: No, brother, for this last wrong is greater than the first (ancient Greek)
decisions.reason: Tamar's words are hard to read in the Hebrew, as if spoken in distress, and the first words ("no, because of") do not fit together easily. The sense is clear enough: to send her away would be a greater wrong than the rape itself. The ancient Greek translation reads roughly "No, brother, for this last wrong is greater than the first", which may reflect a slightly different Hebrew text. The Hebrew is followed here; reviewers should check the Greek wording against an edition.

decisions.choice: to send me away: what the law forbade such a man to do
decisions.reason: The law said that a man who seized and lay with an unmarried girl must marry her and "may not send her away all his days" (Deuteronomy 22:29; see also Exodus 22:15). Amnon does the very thing the law forbade, and leaves her disgraced and without a husband. The verb returns in verse 17.

decisions.choice: he was not willing to listen to her: as in verse 14
decisions.reason: The narrator repeats the words of verse 14. A second time, her plea goes unheard.

decisions.choice: Sending me away would be a greater wrong
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the sending away at the front so the comparison is clear. Literal follows the Hebrew order and brackets "is worse", which the Hebrew leaves to be understood.

records.source: וַיִּקְרָ֗א אֶֽת־נַעֲרוֹ֙ מְשָׁ֣רְת֔וֹ וַיֹּ֕אמֶר שִׁלְחוּ־נָ֥א אֶת־זֹ֛את מֵעָלַ֖י הַח֑וּצָה וּנְעֹ֥ל הַדֶּ֖לֶת אַחֲרֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And he called his young man, his attendant, and said, send away please this from with me outside, and bolt the door after her.
pieces: He called the young man who attended him and said, "Put this woman out of my room, and bolt the door behind her."

L.17: And he called his young man who served him and said, "Please send this [woman] away from me, outside, and bolt the door after her."

R.17: He called his personal servant and said, "Get this woman out of here! Lock the door behind her!"

decisions.choice: this: a word of contempt
decisions.reason: Amnon does not name her or call her his sister; he says only "this" (a feminine form, "this one"). The bare word shows his scorn.

decisions.choice: his young man who served him: his personal attendant
decisions.reason: The two words name a young man in his personal service. He is the only witness of how Tamar was thrown out.

decisions.choice: send away: the verb of verse 16
decisions.reason: Amnon gives the very order Tamar has just begged him not to give, and has his servant carry it out.

decisions.choice: Put this woman out of my room (Balanced); Get this woman out of here (Readable)
decisions.reason: The "please" in Amnon's order is a matter of form, and Balanced and Readable leave it out. "Woman" is supplied at every level for the bare "this", which English cannot use alone; Literal brackets it.

records.source: וְעָלֶ֨יהָ֙ כְּתֹ֣נֶת פַּסִּ֔ים כִּי֩ כֵ֨ן תִּלְבַּ֧שְׁןָ בְנוֹת־הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ הַבְּתוּלֹ֖ת מְעִילִ֑ים וַיֹּצֵ֨א אוֹתָ֤הּ מְשָֽׁרְתוֹ֙ הַח֔וּץ וְנָעַ֥ל הַדֶּ֖לֶת אַחֲרֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And on her [was] a tunic of passim, for thus were clothed [the] daughters of the king, the virgins, [in] robes; and brought her out his attendant outside and bolted the door after her.
pieces: She was wearing a long-sleeved robe, the kind of robe the king's unmarried daughters wore. His servant put her out and bolted the door behind her.

L.18: Now she had on her a tunic [reaching to the] wrists [and ankles], for the virgin daughters of the king were clothed [in] such robes. And his attendant brought her outside and bolted the door after her.

R.18: Tamar was wearing a special robe with long sleeves. The king's daughters who were not yet married wore robes like that. Amnon's servant put her outside and locked the door behind her.

decisions.choice: a tunic of passim: a long robe reaching to the wrists and ankles
decisions.reason: Passim probably means "palms (of the hands) and soles (of the feet)": a full-length robe with long sleeves, as worn by those who did no hard work. It is the same garment Jacob gave Joseph (Genesis 37:3), the only other place it is named. The ancient Greek translation took it to mean a robe reaching the wrists here and "many-colored" in Genesis; the length and sleeves, not the color, seem to be the point.

decisions.choice: the virgin daughters of the king: the robe marked her rank and her state
decisions.reason: The robe showed that she was a king's daughter and unmarried. The narrator pauses to describe it just as she is thrown out, so that the reader sees what has been taken from her; in verse 19 she tears it.

decisions.choice: robes: the outer garments
decisions.reason: The word names a robe or mantle worn over other clothes (1 Samuel 18:4; 24:5). Its place at the end of the clause is awkward in Hebrew, and some suggest it is a slightly changed form of "from long ago" ("so the king's daughters had dressed from of old"). The sense of the verse is not affected.

decisions.choice: a tunic [reaching to the] wrists [and ankles] (Literal); a long-sleeved robe (Balanced); a special robe with long sleeves (Readable)
decisions.reason: The same wording as for Joseph's robe in Genesis 37:3, so that readers can see the link. The familiar "coat of many colors" follows the Greek translation of Genesis.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: The word for the attendant of verse 17 is "one who serves"; Balanced and Readable say "servant". Readable names him as Amnon's servant, since "his" could seem to point to someone else.

records.source: וַתִּקַּ֨ח תָּמָ֥ר אֵ֨פֶר֙ עַל־רֹאשָׁ֔הּ וּכְתֹ֧נֶת הַפַּסִּ֛ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָלֶ֖יהָ קָרָ֑עָה וַתָּ֤שֶׂם יָדָהּ֙ עַל־רֹאשָׁ֔הּ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ הָל֖וֹךְ וְזָעָֽקָה׃
records.gloss: And took Tamar ashes on her head, and the tunic of passim which [was] on her she tore, and put her hand on her head and went, going and crying out.
pieces: Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long-sleeved robe she was wearing. She put her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.

L.19: And Tamar put ashes on her head, and she tore the tunic [reaching to the] wrists [and ankles] that [was] on her, and she put her hand on her head and went away, crying out as she went.

R.19: Tamar put ashes on her head and tore her special robe with long sleeves. She put her hand on her head to show her grief. Then she went away, crying loudly.

decisions.choice: ashes on her head; tore the robe: signs of mourning
decisions.reason: Putting dust or ashes on the head and tearing clothes were the usual signs of grief and disaster (1:2; Joshua 7:6). Tearing the robe that marked her as a king's virgin daughter shows what she has lost.

decisions.choice: put her hand on her head: a gesture of grief and shame
decisions.reason: The same gesture is named in Jeremiah 2:37, of people led away in disgrace.

decisions.choice: went, going and crying out: she cried out as she went, openly
decisions.reason: The verb "go" is doubled, describing an action that went on: she kept crying out as she walked. In the law, a woman's cry for help is what shows that she was forced (Deuteronomy 22:24, 27). Tamar does not hide what has happened.

decisions.choice: to show her grief
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the gesture meant.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלֶ֜יהָ אַבְשָׁל֣וֹם אָחִ֗יהָ הַאֲמִינ֣וֹן אָחִיךְ֮ הָיָ֣ה עִמָּךְ֒ וְעַתָּ֞ה אֲחוֹתִ֤י הַחֲרִ֨ישִׁי֙ אָחִ֣יךְ ה֔וּא אַל־תָּשִׁ֥יתִי אֶת־לִבֵּ֖ךְ לַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַתֵּ֤שֶׁב תָּמָר֙ וְשֹׁ֣מֵמָ֔ה בֵּ֖ית אַבְשָׁל֥וֹם אָחִֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And said to her Absalom her brother, [has] Aminon your brother been with you? And now, my sister, be silent; your brother [is] he; do not set your heart to this thing. And dwelt Tamar, and desolate, [in the] house of Absalom her brother.
pieces: Absalom, her brother, asked her, "Has your brother Amnon been with you? Now, my sister, keep quiet. He is your brother. Do not take this matter to heart." So Tamar lived in her brother Absalom's house, a desolate woman.

L.20: And Absalom her brother said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? But now, my sister, keep silent; he [is] your brother. Do not set your heart on this matter." And Tamar dwelt, a desolate [woman], in the house of Absalom her brother.

R.20: Her brother Absalom asked her, "Has your brother Amnon done this to you? Now, my sister, say nothing about it. He is your brother. Do not let it break your heart." So Tamar lived on in her brother Absalom's house, alone and in despair.

decisions.choice: been with you: had sexual relations with you
decisions.reason: Absalom guesses at once what has happened and puts it in a restrained way. He asks about "Amnon your brother", setting the deed beside the family bond.

decisions.choice: Aminon: a different form of Amnon's name
decisions.reason: Here alone the Hebrew spells the name Aminon. It may be a scornful little name on Absalom's lips, or just another spelling. It is the same man.

decisions.choice: keep silent; he is your brother; do not set your heart on this: Absalom tells her to bear it quietly
decisions.reason: To "set the heart" on something is to dwell on it or brood over it (verse 33). Absalom's counsel sounds like comfort, but verses 22 and 32 show that he was nursing his own plan in silence.

decisions.choice: desolate: ruined, left alone and without hope of marriage
decisions.reason: The word is used of a land laid waste and of a woman left without husband or children (Isaiah 54:1). Tamar lived on in her brother's house, unmarried and childless, cut off from the life she might have had.

decisions.choice: Amnon
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the usual spelling of the name so that readers are not confused; the meaning decision notes the different Hebrew form.

decisions.choice: done this to you; let it break your heart; alone and in despair
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what Absalom's question means, puts "set your heart on" as letting it break her heart, and explains "desolate" in two simple words.

records.source: וְהַמֶּ֣לֶךְ דָּוִ֔ד שָׁמַ֕ע אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּ֥חַר ל֖וֹ מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: And the king David heard all the things the these, and it burned to him greatly.
pieces: When King David heard about all these things, he was very angry.

L.21: And King David heard all these things, and he burned [with anger] greatly.

R.21: When King David heard about all this, he was furious.

decisions.choice: the Hebrew text ends with David's anger
alternatives: adds: but he did not trouble his son Amnon, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn (ancient Greek; Qumran)
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation, and a Hebrew manuscript of Samuel from Qumran as far as it can be read, add: "but he did not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son, because he loved him, for he was his firstborn." This would explain why David did nothing. The Hebrew text, which does not have the words, is followed here. The longer reading may be original and have dropped out by a copying slip, or may be an early explanation added to the text. Reviewers should check these readings against the textual evidence.

decisions.choice: it burned to him: he became angry
decisions.reason: Anger is pictured as heat rising in a person, as in 12:5 when David heard Nathan's story.

decisions.choice: very angry, but he does nothing
decisions.reason: The text tells of David's anger but of no punishment for Amnon. Eli was blamed for not restraining his sons (1 Samuel 3:13), and of David's son Adonijah it is later said that his father had never crossed him (1 Kings 1:6). Absalom's silence (verse 22) fills the gap David leaves.

decisions.choice: burned [with anger]
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the picture of burning and brackets "with anger", which the Hebrew leaves to be understood.

records.source: וְלֹֽא־דִבֶּ֧ר אַבְשָׁל֛וֹם עִם־אַמְנ֖וֹן לְמֵרָ֣ע וְעַד־ט֑וֹב כִּֽי־שָׂנֵ֤א אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ אֶת־אַמְנ֔וֹן עַל־דְּבַר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עִנָּ֔ה אֵ֖ת תָּמָ֥ר אֲחֹתֽוֹ׃פ
records.gloss: And not spoke Absalom with Amnon from bad to good, for hated Absalom Amnon over [the] matter that he had humbled Tamar his sister.
pieces: Absalom said nothing at all to Amnon, good or bad. He hated Amnon because he had violated his sister Tamar.

L.22: And Absalom did not speak with Amnon, either bad or good, for Absalom hated Amnon on account of his having humbled Tamar his sister.

R.22: Absalom did not say one word to Amnon, good or bad. He hated Amnon for raping his sister Tamar.

decisions.choice: from bad to good: nothing at all
decisions.reason: Naming two opposites covers everything between them. Absalom said nothing to Amnon of any kind, as Laban was told to say nothing to Jacob "good or bad" (Genesis 31:24, 29).

decisions.choice: humbled: violated
decisions.reason: The verb of verses 12 and 14.

decisions.choice: he hated Amnon: Absalom's silence hides his hatred
decisions.reason: The verb "hated" is the one used of Amnon's hatred for Tamar in verse 15. Absalom's silence is not peace but a hatred kept hidden, which waits two years (verse 23). "His sister" can be read as Absalom's or Amnon's; she was both.

decisions.choice: violated (Balanced); raping (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verses 12 and 14.

records.source: וַֽיְהִי֙ לִשְׁנָתַ֣יִם יָמִ֔ים וַיִּהְי֤וּ גֹֽזְזִים֙ לְאַבְשָׁל֔וֹם בְּבַ֥עַל חָצ֖וֹר אֲשֶׁ֣ר עִם־אֶפְרָ֑יִם וַיִּקְרָ֥א אַבְשָׁל֖וֹם לְכָל־בְּנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And it was after two years [of] days, and there were shearers for Absalom in Baal-hazor, which [is] near Ephraim; and invited Absalom all [the] sons of the king.
pieces: Two full years later, Absalom had sheepshearers at work at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and he invited all the king's sons.

L.23: And it happened after two full years that Absalom had sheepshearers in Baal-hazor, which [is] near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the sons of the king.

R.23: Two whole years later, Absalom's sheep were being sheared at Baal-hazor, near the town of Ephraim. Absalom invited all the king's sons to the celebration.

decisions.choice: two years of days: two full years
decisions.reason: Adding "days" to a length of time means the whole of it (Genesis 41:1). Absalom has waited two years in silence since verse 22.

decisions.choice: sheepshearers: the season of shearing, a time of feasting
decisions.reason: Shearing time was a festival for flock owners, with food and wine for the household and guests (1 Samuel 25:2, 8, 36; Genesis 38:12). Absalom's invitation would seem natural.

decisions.choice: Baal-hazor near Ephraim: a place in the hills north of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Baal-hazor is usually identified with a high hill about fifteen miles north of Jerusalem. "Ephraim" here is probably a town near it (perhaps the Ephraim of John 11:54), rather than the tribe, whose land lay further north.

decisions.choice: Absalom's sheep were being sheared; to the celebration
decisions.reason: Readable explains "Absalom had sheepshearers" and adds what the invitation was to, from the custom described in the meaning decision.

records.heading: Absalom kills Amnon

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֤א אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּה־נָ֥א גֹזְזִ֖ים לְעַבְדֶּ֑ךָ יֵֽלֶךְ־נָ֥א הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ וַעֲבָדָ֖יו עִם־עַבְדֶּֽךָ׃
records.gloss: And came Absalom to the king and said, look please, shearers [are] to your servant; let go please the king and his servants with your servant.
pieces: Absalom came to the king and said, "Your servant has sheepshearers at work. Will the king and his officials please come with your servant?"

L.24: And Absalom came to the king and said, "Look, please, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant."

R.24: Absalom went to the king and said, "Your servant is having his sheep sheared. Please come, my king, and bring your officials with you."

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "I" to the king
decisions.reason: Speaking to a king, a subject referred to himself as "your servant" (9:2; 1 Samuel 20:7-8). Absalom also speaks of David as "the king" rather than "you", as court courtesy required.

decisions.choice: the king and his servants: the king and his court
decisions.reason: "His servants" are David's officials. To invite the king and his whole court was a great honor to offer, and it made the feast seem innocent.

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: As in 1 Samuel, the polite "your servant" is kept at every level. Readable keeps it once and then speaks to the king directly.

decisions.choice: officials
decisions.reason: The king's servants here are his court officials, so Balanced and Readable say "officials"; Literal keeps "servants".

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אֶל־אַבְשָׁל֗וֹם אַל־בְּנִי֙ אַל־נָ֤א נֵלֵךְ֙ כֻּלָּ֔נוּ וְלֹ֥א נִכְבַּ֖ד עָלֶ֑יךָ וַיִּפְרָץ־בּ֛וֹ וְלֹֽא־אָבָ֥ה לָלֶ֖כֶת וַֽיְבָרֲכֵֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And said the king to Absalom, no, my son, let us not go please all of us, and not we will be heavy on you. And he urged him, but not he was willing to go, and he blessed him.
pieces: "No, my son," the king said to Absalom. "We should not all go; we would only be a burden to you." Absalom pressed him, but he would not go, though he gave him his blessing.

L.25: And the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, so that we will not be heavy on you." And he urged him, but he was not willing to go, and he blessed him.

R.25: But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son. We will not all come. It would cost you too much." Absalom kept asking him, but the king still would not go. Instead he gave Absalom his blessing and sent him off.

decisions.choice: be heavy on you: be a burden, a cost to you
decisions.reason: To feed and lodge the king and his whole court would have cost a great deal. David refuses kindly, out of concern for his son.

decisions.choice: urged him: pressed him hard
decisions.reason: The verb means to break through. Here it describes insistent pleading; it returns in verse 27.

decisions.choice: blessed him: gave him his good wishes as he left
decisions.reason: A blessing was often given when someone took leave (Genesis 47:10; 2 Samuel 19:40). David sends Absalom off with his goodwill, unaware of what is planned.

decisions.choice: It would cost you too much; and sent him off
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "be heavy on you" means and adds that the blessing was a farewell, as the meaning decision explains.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אַבְשָׁל֔וֹם וָלֹ֕א יֵֽלֶךְ־נָ֥א אִתָּ֖נוּ אַמְנ֣וֹן אָחִ֑י וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לָ֥מָּה יֵלֵ֖ךְ עִמָּֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And said Absalom, and if not, let go please with us Amnon my brother. And said to him the king, why should he go with you?
pieces: Then Absalom said, "If you will not come, then please let my brother Amnon go with us." The king asked him, "Why should he go with you?"

L.26: And Absalom said, "If not, please let Amnon my brother go with us." And the king said to him, "Why should he go with you?"

R.26: Then Absalom said, "If you will not come, please let my brother Amnon come with us." The king asked, "Why should he go with you?"

decisions.choice: and if not: if you will not come
decisions.reason: The short words mean "if you will not go yourself". Absalom has been aiming at this request all along.

decisions.choice: Amnon my brother: the king's firstborn, as the king's stand-in
decisions.reason: Amnon was David's eldest son and heir (3:2). If the king would not come, it would seem fitting for his firstborn to come in his place. Absalom calls him "my brother" while planning his death.

decisions.choice: why should he go with you: the king hesitates
decisions.reason: The question may show that David sensed something wrong, or only that he saw no need. The text does not say, but he gives way in verse 27.

decisions.choice: If you will not come
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out the bare "if not".

records.source: וַיִּפְרָץ־בּ֖וֹ אַבְשָׁל֑וֹם וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אִתּוֹ֙ אֶת־אַמְנ֔וֹן וְאֵ֖ת כָּל־בְּנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃ס
records.gloss: And urged him Absalom, and he sent with him Amnon and all [the] sons of the king.
pieces: But Absalom kept pressing him, so he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.

L.27: And Absalom urged him, and he sent Amnon and all the sons of the king with him.

R.27: But Absalom kept on asking, so the king let Amnon and all his other sons go with Absalom.

decisions.choice: the Hebrew text ends with the sending of the king's sons
alternatives: adds: And Absalom made a feast like a king's feast (ancient Greek; Qumran)
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation, supported by a Hebrew manuscript from Qumran, adds: "And Absalom made a feast like the feast of a king." The added words fit the story and recall Nabal's feast at shearing time (1 Samuel 25:36), but the Hebrew text is followed here. Reviewers should check the readings.

decisions.choice: urged him: as in verse 25
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 25. This time the king gives way.

decisions.choice: all his other sons
decisions.reason: Readable says "other" because Amnon has just been named, and names Absalom where "him" could be unclear.

records.source: וַיְצַו֩ אַבְשָׁל֨וֹם אֶת־נְעָרָ֜יו לֵאמֹ֗ר רְא֣וּ נָ֠א כְּט֨וֹב לֵב־אַמְנ֤וֹן בַּיַּ֨יִן֙ וְאָמַרְתִּ֣י אֲלֵיכֶ֔ם הַכּ֧וּ אֶת־אַמְנ֛וֹן וַהֲמִתֶּ֥ם אֹת֖וֹ אַל־תִּירָ֑אוּ הֲל֗וֹא כִּ֤י אָֽנֹכִי֙ צִוִּ֣יתִי אֶתְכֶ֔ם חִזְק֖וּ וִהְי֥וּ לִבְנֵי־חָֽיִל׃
records.gloss: And commanded Absalom his young men, saying, see please, when [is] good [the] heart of Amnon with wine, and I say to you, strike Amnon, and you will kill him; do not fear; [is it] not that I, I have commanded you? Be strong and be sons of valor.
pieces: Absalom gave his servants these orders: "Watch closely. When Amnon is in high spirits from the wine and I tell you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not be afraid. Have I not given you the order myself? Be strong and act like brave men."

L.28: And Absalom commanded his young men, saying, "See now: when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not be afraid. Have not I myself commanded you? Be strong and be sons of valor."

R.28: Absalom gave orders to his servants. "Listen," he said. "Wait until Amnon has drunk a lot of wine and is feeling happy. Then I will say to you, 'Kill Amnon!' When I do, kill him. Do not be afraid. I am the one giving you the order. Be strong and brave!"

decisions.choice: when Amnon's heart is good with wine: when he is merry and drunk
decisions.reason: A "good heart" with wine means being cheerful from drinking (1 Samuel 25:36, of Nabal at his shearing feast; Esther 1:10). Amnon would be off his guard.

decisions.choice: have not I myself commanded you: the responsibility is mine
decisions.reason: "I" is stressed in the Hebrew. Absalom takes the guilt on himself, so his men need not fear to strike the king's son.

decisions.choice: be sons of valor: be brave men
decisions.reason: A "son of" a quality is someone who has it. "Sons of valor" are men who are brave and able to fight (1 Samuel 18:17).

decisions.choice: his young men: his servants
decisions.reason: The word means young men, and often young men in someone's service. Here they are Absalom's own men, whom he can command (verse 29).

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "young men"; Balanced and Readable say "servants", their place here.

decisions.choice: has drunk a lot of wine and is feeling happy; Kill Amnon
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom and puts the order "strike" as "kill", which is what Absalom means, as the next words show.

records.source: וַֽיַּעֲשׂ֞וּ נַעֲרֵ֤י אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ לְאַמְנ֔וֹן כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר צִוָּ֖ה אַבְשָׁל֑וֹם וַיָּקֻ֣מוּ׀כָּל־בְּנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ וַֽיִּרְכְּב֛וּ אִ֥ישׁ עַל־פִּרְדּ֖וֹ וַיָּנֻֽסוּ׃
records.gloss: And did [the] young men of Absalom to Amnon just as had commanded Absalom; and arose all [the] sons of the king and rode each on his mule and fled.
pieces: So Absalom's servants did to Amnon exactly what Absalom had ordered. Then all the king's sons got up, mounted their mules and fled.

L.29: And the young men of Absalom did to Amnon just as Absalom had commanded. And all the sons of the king rose up, and each mounted his mule, and they fled.

R.29: So Absalom's servants killed Amnon, just as Absalom had ordered. Then all the king's other sons jumped up, got on their mules and rode away as fast as they could.

decisions.choice: did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded: they killed him
decisions.reason: The narrator does not describe the killing; the order in verse 28 has already said what was to be done.

decisions.choice: mule: the mount of the royal family
decisions.reason: Mules were costly animals ridden by the king's household (18:9; 1 Kings 1:33, 38). Each son rode his own.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: As in verse 28.

decisions.choice: killed Amnon; other sons; as fast as they could
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the servants did, makes clear that Amnon is not among those who fled, and brings out the haste in "fled".

records.source: וַֽיְהִי֙ הֵ֣מָּה בַדֶּ֔רֶךְ וְהַשְּׁמֻעָ֣ה בָ֔אָה אֶל־דָּוִ֖ד לֵאמֹ֑ר הִכָּ֤ה אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ אֶת־כָּל־בְּנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְלֹֽא־נוֹתַ֥ר מֵהֶ֖ם אֶחָֽד׃ס
records.gloss: And it was, they [were] on the way, and the report came to David, saying, struck Absalom all [the] sons of the king, and not is left of them one.
pieces: While they were still on the road, the report reached David: "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons; not one of them is left!"

L.30: And while they [were] on the way, the report came to David, saying, "Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king, and not one of them is left."

R.30: While they were still on their way, news reached David: "Absalom has killed all the king's sons! Not one of them is left alive!"

decisions.choice: the report: news passed on by word of mouth
decisions.reason: The word means something heard. It ran ahead of the king's sons and, as rumors do, made the disaster greater than it was.

decisions.choice: while they were on the way: the rumor arrives first
decisions.reason: The king's sons fleeing on mules took some time to reach Jerusalem, and the rumor outran them.

decisions.choice: left alive
decisions.reason: Readable adds "alive" to make the sense of "left" plain.

records.source: וַיָּ֧קָם הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ וַיִּקְרַ֥ע אֶת־בְּגָדָ֖יו וַיִּשְׁכַּ֣ב אָ֑רְצָה וְכָל־עֲבָדָ֥יו נִצָּבִ֖ים קְרֻעֵ֥י בְגָדִֽים׃ס
records.gloss: And arose the king and tore his garments and lay [on the] ground, and all his servants [were] standing, torn of garments.
pieces: The king rose, tore his clothes and lay on the ground. All his officials stood beside him with their clothes torn.

L.31: And the king rose and tore his garments and lay on the ground, and all his servants [were] standing [by with their] garments torn.

R.31: The king stood up and tore his clothes in grief. Then he lay down on the ground. All his officials stood beside him, and they had torn their clothes too.

decisions.choice: tore his garments and lay on the ground: the signs of deepest mourning
decisions.reason: Tearing one's clothes and lying on the ground showed grief and helplessness (1:11; 12:16). The officials join their king in mourning.

decisions.choice: officials
decisions.reason: The king's servants are his court officials, as in verse 24.

decisions.choice: in grief
decisions.reason: Readable gives the reason for the custom.

records.source: וַיַּ֡עַן יוֹנָדָ֣ב׀בֶּן־שִׁמְעָ֨ה אֲחִֽי־דָוִ֜ד וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אַל־יֹאמַ֤ר אֲדֹנִי֙ אֵ֣ת כָּל־הַנְּעָרִ֤ים בְּנֵֽי־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ הֵמִ֔יתוּ כִּֽי־אַמְנ֥וֹן לְבַדּ֖וֹ מֵ֑ת כִּֽי־עַל־פִּ֤י אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ הָיְתָ֣ה שׂוּמָ֔ה מִיּוֹם֙ עַנֹּת֔וֹ אֵ֖ת תָּמָ֥ר אֲחֹתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And answered Jonadab son of Shimeah, brother of David, and said, let not say my lord, all the young men, the sons of the king, they have killed, for Amnon alone has died; for on [the] mouth of Absalom it has been set from [the] day of his humbling Tamar his sister.
pieces: But Jonadab son of Shimeah, David's brother, spoke up: "My lord should not think they have killed all the young men, the king's sons. Only Amnon is dead. Absalom has been determined to do this ever since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.

L.32: And Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, answered and said, "Let not my lord say [that] they have killed all the young men, the sons of the king, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the mouth of Absalom this has been set from the day that he humbled Tamar his sister.

R.32: But Jonadab spoke up. He was the son of David's brother Shimeah. "My lord, do not think that all the young princes have been killed. Only Amnon is dead. Absalom has been planning this ever since the day Amnon raped his sister Tamar.

decisions.choice: on the mouth of Absalom it has been set: Absalom has been resolved on this
alternatives: by Absalom's command it was decided
it could be seen on Absalom's face
decisions.reason: The phrase is unusual. It may mean that the killing was settled by Absalom's own word ("mouth" as in a command), or that it was written on his face, as if his look had shown it since that day. Either way Jonadab says that Absalom had meant to do this for two years.

decisions.choice: let not my lord say: my lord should not think
decisions.reason: "Say" here means to say to oneself, to think or suppose.

decisions.choice: Jonadab: the man who planned Amnon's trick
decisions.reason: The "shrewd" friend of verses 3-5 now knows the mind of the other side as well. He who gave Amnon the plan that led to this speaks calmly to the grieving king.

decisions.choice: his humbling Tamar: Amnon's rape of Tamar
decisions.reason: The verb of verses 12, 14 and 22.

decisions.choice: Absalom has been determined to do this (Balanced); Absalom has been planning this (Readable); violated / raped
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom without choosing between its two pictures. They name Amnon where the Hebrew says "he", and say "violated" and "raped" as in verses 12-22. Readable puts "the young men, the sons of the king" as "the young princes".

records.source: וְעַתָּ֡ה אַל־יָשֵׂם֩ אֲדֹנִ֨י הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֶל־לִבּוֹ֙ דָּבָ֣ר לֵאמֹ֔ר כָּל־בְּנֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מֵ֑תוּ כִּֽי־אִם־אַמְנ֥וֹן לְבַדּ֖וֹ מֵֽת׃פ
records.gloss: And now let not set my lord the king to his heart a word, saying, all [the] sons of the king have died; for only Amnon alone has died.
pieces: So now, my lord the king should not take to heart the report that all the king's sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead."

L.33: And now let not my lord the king take the thing to his heart, saying, 'All the sons of the king are dead,' for only Amnon alone is dead."

R.33: So, my king, do not believe the news that all your sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead."

decisions.choice: set to his heart: take seriously, be troubled by
decisions.reason: To set something to the heart is to dwell on it and let it weigh on one (verse 20). Jonadab tells the king not to believe the rumor.

decisions.choice: only Amnon alone: the point is repeated
decisions.reason: Jonadab says it a second time (verse 32), with two words for "only", to calm the king.

decisions.choice: do not believe the news
decisions.reason: Readable puts the idiom "set to his heart" as not believing the report, which is its sense here.

records.source: וַיִּבְרַ֖ח אַבְשָׁל֑וֹם וַיִּשָּׂ֞א הַנַּ֤עַר הַצֹּפֶה֙ אֶת־עֵינָ֔יו וַיַּ֗רְא וְהִנֵּ֨ה עַם־רַ֜ב הֹלְכִ֥ים מִדֶּ֛רֶךְ אַחֲרָ֖יו מִצַּ֥ד הָהָֽר׃
records.gloss: And fled Absalom. And lifted the young man, the watchman, his eyes and saw, and look, many people [were] coming from [the] road behind him from [the] side of the mountain.
pieces: Meanwhile Absalom fled. The young man on watch looked up and saw many people coming along the road behind him, down the side of the hill.

L.34: And Absalom fled. And the young man who was keeping watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and look, many people [were] coming from the road behind him, from the side of the hill.

R.34: Meanwhile, Absalom ran away. The young man on guard looked out and saw a large crowd coming down the hillside on the road behind him.

decisions.choice: Absalom fled: a brief aside
decisions.reason: The narrator breaks off to say what Absalom did while the king mourned. The same words return in verses 37 and 38.

decisions.choice: the road behind him: a road coming from behind the watchman
alternatives: from the road to the west
from the road of Horonaim (ancient Greek)
decisions.reason: "Behind" may simply mean behind the watchman as he faced out, or it may mean "west", since the Hebrew way of giving directions faced east, with the west behind. The ancient Greek translation reads "the road of Horonaim" and adds the watchman's report to the king; it may reflect a fuller Hebrew text. The Hebrew is followed here; reviewers should check the Greek.

decisions.choice: the young man keeping watch: a lookout on the city wall
decisions.reason: A watchman stood on the wall or gate tower to report anyone approaching the city (18:24-27).

decisions.choice: looked up (Balanced); looked out (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Lifted up his eyes" is the Hebrew way of saying someone looked. Balanced and Readable leave out the second "look", which only draws attention to the sight.

records.heading: Absalom flees

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יֽוֹנָדָב֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ הִנֵּ֥ה בְנֵֽי־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בָּ֑אוּ כִּדְבַ֥ר עַבְדְּךָ֖ כֵּ֥ן הָיָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said Jonadab to the king, look, [the] sons of the king have come; according to [the] word of your servant, so it has happened.
pieces: Jonadab said to the king, "See, the king's sons are here! It has happened just as your servant said."

L.35: And Jonadab said to the king, "Look, the sons of the king have come! As your servant said, so it has happened."

R.35: Jonadab said to the king, "Look, your sons are coming! It is just as I, your servant, told you."

decisions.choice: your servant: Jonadab speaks of himself politely
decisions.reason: As in verse 24, a subject speaking to the king calls himself "your servant". Jonadab claims credit for being right.

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: Kept at every level, as in verse 24; Readable adds "I" so the reader sees that Jonadab means himself.

decisions.choice: your sons
decisions.reason: Readable says "your sons", since Jonadab is speaking to their father.

records.source: וַיְהִ֣י׀כְּכַלֹּת֣וֹ לְדַבֵּ֗ר וְהִנֵּ֤ה בְנֵֽי־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ בָּ֔אוּ וַיִּשְׂא֥וּ קוֹלָ֖ם וַיִּבְכּ֑וּ וְגַם־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְכָל־עֲבָדָ֔יו בָּכ֕וּ בְּכִ֖י גָּד֥וֹל מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: And it was, as he finished speaking, and look, [the] sons of the king came and lifted up their voice and wept; and also the king and all his servants wept [with] a weeping great very.
pieces: He had hardly finished speaking when the king's sons came in, weeping aloud. The king and all his officials also wept very bitterly.

L.36: And it happened, as he finished speaking, that look, the sons of the king came, and they lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept [with] a very great weeping.

R.36: He had just finished speaking when the king's sons arrived. They were crying loudly. The king and all his officials cried bitterly too.

decisions.choice: lifted up their voice and wept: wept aloud
decisions.reason: The phrase describes loud weeping, the open grief of mourning (Genesis 29:11; Judges 2:4).

decisions.choice: wept with a very great weeping: the grief was deep
decisions.reason: The verb is followed by its own noun and "very great", the strongest way Hebrew has to say it. Relief that the sons are alive is swallowed up in grief for Amnon.

decisions.choice: officials
decisions.reason: As in verse 31.

records.source: וְאַבְשָׁל֣וֹם בָּרַ֔ח וַיֵּ֛לֶךְ אֶל־תַּלְמַ֥י בֶּן־עַמִּיה֖וּד מֶ֣לֶךְ גְּשׁ֑וּר וַיִּתְאַבֵּ֥ל עַל־בְּנ֖וֹ כָּל־הַיָּמִֽים׃
records.gloss: And Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And he mourned over his son all the days.
pieces: Absalom fled; he went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. David grieved for his son day after day.

L.37: And Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And he mourned for his son all the days.

R.37: Absalom ran away to Talmai son of Ammihud, the king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son Amnon day after day.

decisions.choice: Talmai king of Geshur: Absalom's grandfather
decisions.reason: Absalom's mother Maacah was the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (3:3), a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee. Absalom fled to his mother's family, beyond David's reach.

decisions.choice: Ammihud: the name as the scribes' notes read it
decisions.reason: The Hebrew letters spell the name Ammihur, and the scribes' notes read it as Ammihud. The text follows the reading of the notes, as the data does.

decisions.choice: he mourned for his son: David mourned for Amnon
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not name the one who mourned or the son. David is the one who can mourn "his son", and in verse 39 he is comforted for Amnon, so Amnon is most likely meant. Some take the son to be Absalom, now lost to him in exile.

decisions.choice: all the days: day after day, for a long time
decisions.reason: The phrase means continually, for the time that followed.

decisions.choice: David (Balanced, Readable); Amnon (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name David as the one who mourned, and Readable names the son, following the meaning decision. Literal keeps the Hebrew "he" and "his son".

records.gloss: And Absalom fled and went [to] Geshur, and he was there three years.
pieces: So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and he stayed there three years.

L.38: And Absalom fled and went [to] Geshur, and he was there three years.

R.38: After Absalom ran away to Geshur, he stayed there for three years.

decisions.choice: Absalom fled: the third time
decisions.reason: The words "Absalom fled" come for the third time (verses 34, 37). The repetition closes the story of his flight and leads to the three years of exile.

decisions.choice: After Absalom ran away to Geshur, he stayed there
decisions.reason: Readable joins the two clauses with "after" to show the order of events.

records.gloss: And it was finished [?] David the king to go out to Absalom, for he was comforted over Amnon, for he was dead.
pieces: And King David longed to go out to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon's death.

L.39: And [the spirit of] King David longed to go out to Absalom, for he was comforted concerning Amnon, since he was dead.

R.39: In time, King David's heart longed to go to Absalom. He had come to accept that Amnon was dead.

decisions.choice: the spirit of King David: something like "spirit" has dropped out
alternatives: David the king (Hebrew as it stands)
decisions.reason: The verb is feminine, but "David the king" is masculine, so the Hebrew seems to have lost a feminine noun such as "the spirit" or "the soul". A Hebrew manuscript from Qumran and the ancient Greek translation read "the spirit of the king". The meaning stays about David's inner self.

decisions.choice: longed to go out to Absalom: David yearned for his exiled son
alternatives: King David ceased to go out against Absalom
King David's anger against Absalom was spent
decisions.reason: The verb means to come to an end, to be spent, and with "spirit" or "soul" it means to long or pine for (Psalm 84:3). The verse can also be read: "King David ceased to go out against Absalom", that is, his anger was spent and he gave up thought of pursuing him. Both readings say that, with Amnon's death behind him, David's heart turned toward Absalom; the first reading is followed. Chapter 14 shows David still not willing to bring Absalom home without being pressed.

decisions.choice: comforted: consoled, his grief eased
decisions.reason: The verb is used of grief that has run its course (Genesis 24:67; 38:12). Time had eased David's mourning for Amnon.

decisions.choice: [the spirit of]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words that the feminine verb seems to need, from the meaning decision. Balanced and Readable say "King David" and "King David's heart", which carry the same sense.

decisions.choice: In time
decisions.reason: Readable adds "In time" to show that this came after the three years of verse 38.
